entries.narration: Every design starts with a line. On one side of the line is the system you are going to build and run: here, a short-link service made of an application and a database. On the other side are the people and systems you merely deal with. Link owners create short links, visitors follow them, and destination sites hold the real pages. You depend on all of them, but you cannot change how any of them behave, and that difference decides what you are responsible for. Notice the dashed arrow. The service tells the visitor's browser where to go, but the browser, not the service, then travels to the destination. Any place where a request crosses the line is an interface, and interfaces are what the rest of this course keeps returning to. A design can also be described at four levels: the context, the deployable parts, the modules inside a part, and the code. Start at the context, and only drop a level when the decision in front of you cannot be made without it. A dependency, by the way, is an outside party you rely on, like the destination site: you can plan to tolerate its failures, but you cannot fix them. And a diagram that mixes levels tends to hide exactly the decision you were trying to make.

The request we were given is four words long: build a URL shortener. That is not a design problem yet, because nobody can say whether a particular system meets it. So we walk each kind of user through what they actually do. The link owner submits a long address, the service checks it is well formed and allowed, stores the pairing of code and address, and hands back a short link. The visitor opens the short link, the service looks the code up, and either redirects them or has to say it does not know that code. That second path is easy to forget, and it is exactly why we draw journeys: every box is a statement we can later test, and every missing branch is a question to ask. Alongside the requirements, we separate two things that are often mixed up. A constraint is a fixed fact we must respect. An assumption is a guess we are choosing to make, like a million daily users. Assumptions are fine, as long as they are written down, because a written assumption can be challenged and changed. We also say plainly what is out of scope for now, so the design stays small.

Functional requirements say what the system does. Quality attributes say how well it has to do it, and they are where most architecture decisions actually come from. The trouble is that wishes like fast, reliable, or safe cannot be met or missed. So each one gets turned into an acceptance criterion with four parts: what is measured, where it is measured, how much is acceptable, and over what window of time. Ninety-nine percent of redirects answered in under one hundred milliseconds, measured at the application over thirty days, is a sentence you can check against real data. Every figure in this table is an assumed target for the lesson, not advice about what any real service should promise. Notice also that the targets pull against each other. Making sure a confirmed link survives the loss of a machine usually costs some latency or some money, so we will have to choose. A missed target is useful, because it points at the part of the design to change, while a quality nobody measured tends to be decided by accident, usually during an outage. The habit to build is simple: write the criterion first, then judge any architecture by whether it can satisfy it.

Capacity estimates look intimidating until you notice they are just a chain of small unit conversions, each with an assumption you can name. We start from a workload we simply declare: one million daily users, each following twenty links. That gives twenty million redirects a day. A day has eighty-six thousand four hundred seconds, so the average works out to about two hundred and thirty-one requests every second. But systems are sized for the busy moments, not the average, so we assume a peak of five times that, roughly one thousand one hundred and fifty-seven requests per second. The same style works for storage. If we assume one new link for every hundred redirects, that is two hundred thousand new links a day, and at an assumed five hundred bytes each, about a hundred megabytes a day, or thirty-six and a half gigabytes a year. Peak response traffic comes to under five megabits a second. Two numbers then play different roles. The peak decides how much capacity must be ready, and the average decides what the system costs to run across the day. A quick sanity check is to multiply back: two hundred and thirty-one times eighty-six thousand four hundred is about twenty million, so the units agree. Now the important part: an average hides how uneven real traffic is, and the five times and five hundred bytes are guesses until someone measures them. The estimate tells you the size of the problem, not the answer.

Latency and throughput are easy to confuse, so let us separate them. Latency is how long a single request takes. Throughput is how many requests complete every second. A system can have good throughput and still make some users wait. This is why we look at percentiles rather than the mean. The curve you see is an illustration, deliberately skewed to the right the way real latency tends to be, with a long tail of slow requests. Its median, the fiftieth percentile, is about thirty-four milliseconds, so half of requests are faster than that. The mean is forty milliseconds and looks respectable. But the ninety-ninth percentile is about a hundred and thirty-three milliseconds, which means one request in a hundred is more than three times slower than the mean suggests. If you only watch the average, you never see those users. The two are linked, too. As a server approaches its limit, requests start to queue and latency rises, so a latency target only holds up to some level of throughput. For a first capacity idea we can use Little's law: the number of requests in flight is roughly the arrival rate times the mean latency. At the peak estimate that is about forty-six requests at the same moment. Be careful with this, though. It is an average-based relationship, and it does not tell you how many requests one server can actually handle.

Now we put the pieces together. The interface on top is what the outside world sees: one call to create a link, which returns a short code, or a clear error if the address is not valid; and one call to follow a code, which redirects the visitor, or answers not found. Those two calls are implemented by a single application, and the application persists everything in a single table. Each row maps a code, which is the primary key and therefore unique, to the long address it stands for, plus the time it was created. Why such a small design? Because our assumed workload, a couple of hundred requests a second on average, is a reasonable place to begin and to measure, and a small design is easy to explain, to test, and to change. The more interesting question is what would make us change it. If measured ninety-ninth percentile latency misses the hundred millisecond target, we would consider caching. If availability falls short of the target, we would consider replicas. If demand outgrows one database, we would consider partitioning. Notice that every one of those changes is tied to a requirement we wrote down. That is the habit this chapter is for. Next, we follow a request across the interfaces and see how communication can fail.

Before a single line of our application runs, the client has to find the server, reach it, and trust it, and every one of those steps costs time. First, DNS turns the name into an IP address. Then the client opens a TCP connection, which costs one round trip. Then it negotiates encryption with TLS, which costs another round trip in version one point three. Only then can it send the actual HTTP request and wait for the answer. Let us put some hypothetical timings on that. Twenty milliseconds for the name lookup, thirty for each handshake, and thirty for the request to travel plus ten for the server's work. Together that is one hundred and twenty milliseconds on a cold connection. But the next request can reuse the open connection, skipping three of those steps, and costs only about forty. This matters for the targets we set in the last chapter. A latency target measured at the application leaves all of this out, yet the visitor still waits for every millisecond of it. It is also the reason connections are kept open and reused.

An API contract starts with naming the things. Our resources are links, so creating one is a post to slash links, reading its details is a get on that link's own address, and the redirect that visitors use is a get on the short code itself. The nouns name what exists, and the HTTP method says what to do with it. Next comes validation. We check input at the boundary, before anything reaches the database: is the scheme allowed, is the address too long, is the host permitted. When the check fails, we need to say so in a way a program can act on. The status code tells the client which class of problem it is: four-hundred-series codes mean the request is wrong, five-hundred-series codes mean we failed. And rather than inventing a new error format for every endpoint, we use one consistent body, following the problem details standard, with an extra field naming which input was at fault. Precision matters because clients make decisions from the status. Unprocessable means fix the request, too many requests means wait, and service unavailable means try again later.

Once other people depend on your API, you cannot change it freely, so three decisions need care. The first is pagination. With offset pagination, the client asks for page three, but if new links are created while they are reading, items shift and some are repeated or skipped. A cursor avoids that by saying resume after this specific item, so inserts elsewhere do not move the place. You should also always cap the page size, because an unbounded list is an easy way to overload the service. The second is versioning. The best approach is to make compatible changes, which keeps old clients working. Adding an optional field, adding a new endpoint, or accepting more input are all compatible. Removing a field, changing a type, or requiring new input will break somebody, and that deserves a new version running beside the old one. The third is how clients read responses. If clients ignore fields they do not recognise, adding a field is safe. A contract is a promise to people you cannot see, so keep it deliberately.

There is no best interface style, only styles that fit particular requirements. REST over HTTP models resources and uses the standard methods, which means browsers, proxies and caches already understand it. RPC is a different idea: you call a named action, like revoke this link. gRPC is RPC carried over HTTP version two with typed schemas, which works well between internal services but is awkward to call directly from a browser. GraphQL lets the client name exactly the fields it wants from a single endpoint. Let us apply that to our service. The public redirect should be a plain HTTP get, because caches understand it and visitors are anonymous. A call from the link service to an internal analytics service could reasonably use gRPC, although plain HTTP would also work. A dashboard whose field needs keep changing might benefit from GraphQL, but you pay for it in harder caching and the need to limit expensive queries. The rule is to pick the simplest option that meets the requirement, not the newest.

A deadline is the total time the caller is willing to wait, and every step along the way spends part of it. Suppose, hypothetically, the caller's deadline is four hundred milliseconds and each attempt times out after a hundred and fifty. If we blindly allow three attempts, that is four hundred and fifty milliseconds of waiting, more than the whole deadline, so the caller has already given up before the last attempt finishes. A sensible loop checks the time left and only retries if it covers another attempt. Between attempts we do not retry immediately. Backoff means waiting longer after each failure, here a hundred milliseconds, then two hundred, then four hundred. Jitter means choosing a random wait up to that limit, so that thousands of clients that failed together do not all retry at the same instant. We also cap the wait and the number of attempts. And there is a cost to be honest about: every retry is more traffic. Three attempts can mean up to three times the load on a dependency that is already struggling, which is how retries turn a small problem into an outage.

Here is the uncomfortable fact behind every retry. A timeout does not mean the operation failed. It only means no answer arrived. Follow the timeline. The client sends a request to create a link. The server receives it, stores the link, and sends back the response, but somewhere on the way the response is lost. From the client's side, this looks exactly the same as the request never arriving at all. So the client faces a dilemma. If it does not retry, the owner may never receive a link, even though one exists. If it does retry and the operation is not idempotent, the server stores a second link, and now one intention has produced two effects. HTTP gives us some guidance. Reading with get is safe, and put and delete are defined as idempotent, meaning repeating them has the same effect as doing them once. Post is not, so our create operation needs extra help. Notice that nothing is broken in either machine. The problem lives in the gap between them.

The standard fix is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique value and sends it with each create request. On the server, inside a single database transaction, we look the key up. If it is already there, we return the stored response and do nothing else. If it is not, we create the link and record the key and the response, all in the same transaction, so that either both rows exist or neither does. That atomicity matters: without it, a crash between the two writes would leave a link with no key. A few edge cases need decisions. If the same key arrives with a different request body, that is a client bug, so we reject it. If two copies arrive at the same moment, the primary key constraint on the key lets only one insert succeed. Keys cannot be kept forever, so they expire after a stated period, which here we assume is twenty-four hours. And be aware that the header is a widely used convention rather than part of core HTTP. There is an alternative design: let the client choose the code and use put, which is idempotent by definition, though then the client must avoid collisions.

Between the visitor and our application there are usually several layers. A reverse proxy receives requests on behalf of the servers behind it. A load balancer spreads those requests across several identical replicas. And health checks let the balancer notice that a replica has stopped answering and quietly stop sending traffic to it, so one failure does not become a visible outage. An edge cache sits even further out and can answer repeat requests without bothering our servers at all, which is attractive for redirects because the same code is requested many times. Here the choice of status code matters. A three-oh-one says the move is permanent, so browsers and caches may keep it for a long time. A three-oh-two is temporary, and is only cached if we explicitly allow it with a cache control header. The trade-off is real: a long cache saves load, but it also delays any change or removal of the link. Finally, remember that every layer adds latency and another thing that can fail, so add each one for a requirement, not by habit.

Let us finish by running three traces through everything in this chapter, on our hypothetical timings. In the first, the create request goes out with an idempotency key, the server stores one row, and a two-hundred-and-one comes back at forty milliseconds on a warm connection. Nothing surprising. In the second, the same request is sent at time zero, but no answer arrives, so the client gives up at a hundred and fifty milliseconds. It waits a jittered sixty milliseconds, then retries at two hundred and ten with the same key. The server finds the key already stored and replays the saved response, so at two hundred and fifty milliseconds the client holds the code, and exactly one link exists. In the third trace, a visitor repeats a get for the short code, and every time they receive the same redirect, because repeating a read changes nothing. Notice that none of the three mechanisms is enough alone. A deadline with no idempotency would create duplicates, and an idempotency key with no deadline would wait forever. The interfaces we have traced all operate on persistent information, so next we turn to how that state should be modelled and stored.

Storage design should begin with what users do, not with a list of tables. Look at the operations. A visitor follows a link, which means the system must find one link given its code. An owner opens a dashboard, which means finding that owner's links, newest first. And a report shows clicks, which means counting by code and by day. Those are the access patterns, the specific ways the data will be asked for. Only then do we decide what entities exist. A link holds a code, a long address, and an owner. A click is an event with a code, a time, and perhaps a referrer. An owner record says who created each link. This order matters because the access patterns decide the keys and the indexes. It also tells us how often each pattern runs. In chapter one we assumed a hundred redirects for every new link, so the redirect lookup will dominate, and that is where we should be most careful. An entity that nobody queries by does not need an index at all.

An invariant is a statement that must be true after every committed change, and good data design starts by writing them down. For our links, every code must map to exactly one long address. Every link must have an address, and we assume a limit of two thousand and forty-eight characters. And every link must belong to an owner who exists. The important question is who enforces these. Application code can check them, but when two requests arrive at the same moment, application checks can both pass and both write, breaking the rule. The database can enforce them reliably, using a primary key for uniqueness, not-null and check constraints for validity, and a foreign key for the owner. We also have to decide the transaction boundary. A transaction makes several changes all-or-nothing, and here the link and its idempotency key from chapter two must share one, so a crash cannot leave one without the other. Keep transactions short, though, because they hold locks that make other requests wait.

Every link needs an identifier, and there are three common strategies. A sequential number encoded in base sixty-two is short and never collides, but anyone can guess the next one and enumerate every link. A random code is hard to guess, but it can collide with one already in use. A hash of the long address gives the same code for the same address, but collisions remain possible. Let us put numbers on random six-character codes. There are about fifty-six point eight billion of them. That sounds enormous, but after a year at our assumed two hundred thousand new links a day, there are seventy-three million links, and about one new code in eight hundred will land on one that already exists. That is roughly two hundred and fifty-seven retries every day. Here is why the uniqueness constraint still matters even when the probability is low: a probability is not a guarantee. With the primary key, a clash becomes a harmless retry. Without it, one unlucky collision would silently overwrite or duplicate a link. And remember that an unguessable code is not access control.

There are two ways to store the same listing. In the normalised design, every fact lives in exactly one place. The owner's display name is stored once, in the owners table, and the links table only holds the owner's identifier. That makes changes simple and consistent: rename an owner in one row and every view of that owner is correct. The price is that a listing which needs both the link and the owner's name must join the two tables. In the denormalised design, we copy the owner's name into each listing row, so showing a listing is a single lookup. The price moves to writes: renaming an owner now means finding and updating every copy, and if one update is missed, the data disagrees with itself. So how should you choose? Normalise by default, because correctness is easier to keep. Denormalise only for a read cost you have actually measured, and when you do, name who is responsible for keeping the copies correct. A stale copy is a bug, unless the requirement explicitly tolerates it.

An index is a sorted copy of some columns that lets the database find rows without reading every one. Without a usable index, a lookup has to scan the whole table, and that cost grows with the table. So we choose indexes by looking at the access patterns from the start of this chapter. Lookup by code is already covered, because the primary key is an index. Listing an owner's links, newest first, wants an index on the owner and the creation time, in that order, so the database can read the first twenty entries and stop. Counting clicks by code and day wants an index on the code and the click time. But indexes are not free. Every insert must also update every index on the table, so each one adds write cost and storage. That is why the table shows a write cost beside every pattern: one extra write per link created, and one per click, which at our peak is over a thousand a second. Finally, check rather than assume. The query plan tells you whether the database actually uses the index. Add an index for a measured need, not for every column.

There are four broad storage models, and each is shaped for particular access patterns. These are typical tendencies, because individual products differ. A relational database gives you tables, joins, constraints and transactions, which is ideal when rules matter, but scaling its writes across machines takes deliberate work. A key-value store is excellent at one thing, looking a value up by its key, such as a code to a long address, but offers little in the way of querying. A document store keeps a nested record together so it can be read and written as one unit, but rules that span several records are often weaker. A wide-column store handles very heavy write volume, with data grouped by key, but you design the tables around the questions you will ask. For our data, the links might be relational, or key-value if lookups dominate and the rules stay simple. The clicks, arriving at hundreds of events a second, might suit a wide-column or other append-friendly store. The rule is to choose by access pattern and invariants, not by fashion.

Beyond the general-purpose models, there are stores built for specialised jobs. A graph database is built for relationships and paths, such as who follows whom. A time-series store is built for values over time, like clicks per minute. A search engine is built for text relevance, ranking and filtering, such as finding links by title. And object storage holds large files cheaply and durably, such as preview images for links. Now ask honestly whether our system needs any of them. The redirect itself needs none of them. Click trends over time might justify a time-series store, and if owners wanted to search their links by title, a search engine might earn its place. But here is the warning. Every additional store is another system to run, to secure, to back up, and to keep in sync with the main database. So add one only when a real requirement appears that the main database cannot meet. The default answer to a new store is not yet.

When the system tells a client that a write succeeded, what exactly have we promised? Each copy of the data protects against a different failure. Flushing the write to disk means it survives a crash of the process. A replica on another machine means it survives losing that machine. But a replica faithfully copies mistakes too, so if someone deletes the wrong rows, the replica deletes them as well. Only a backup, kept separately and from an earlier time, protects against a bad delete or a software bug. And a backup is only real if you have tested restoring from it. Then there is retention. Our assumed policy keeps click events for thirteen months and then deletes them. Retention is a requirement, not an afterthought: someone has to decide how long data is kept and what must be deleted. Finally, think about who may read the data. Raw click records may include IP addresses, which can count as personal data depending on where you operate, so even access to the data is a design decision.

Let us finish by comparing three ways to record clicks, using the workload we assumed in chapter one: twenty million redirects a day, which is about two hundred and thirty-one writes a second on average and over eleven hundred at peak. In model A, every click is a row. At an assumed hundred bytes a row, that is about seven hundred and thirty gigabytes a year, but we keep the raw history and can answer any question later, provided we index it. In model B, we keep a single counter on each link. Storage is tiny and reads are cheap, but a popular link becomes a hot row that every click must update, and we lose all history, so we cannot answer how many clicks per day. Model C keeps raw events for thirteen months and also maintains a daily rollup per code, so dashboards read the small table. The cost is another moving part that can lag. Now suppose we are supplied this evidence: a per-day click query takes eight seconds and the plan shows a full scan. An index on code and click time fixes that query, and the rollup avoids it entirely. We choose C if dashboards matter, and we revisit the decision once we have real measurements. Next, we make the system scale where the evidence says it must.

Scaling a system should start with evidence, and the first question is always which resource is full. There are five places to look. CPU is saturated when the application servers are busy close to all the time. Memory is saturated when the machine starts swapping or the operating system kills processes. Disk shows up as time spent waiting for input and output and as long queues. Network shows up as bandwidth or connection limits. And a dependency, like a database or another service, can be the real bottleneck while every caller above it looks slow. There is a reason to act before a resource reaches one hundred percent. Take a simple queueing model with a service time of ten milliseconds. At fifty percent utilisation a request takes about twenty milliseconds. At eighty percent it takes fifty. At ninety-five percent it takes two hundred. Latency climbs steeply well before the resource is full, which is why a latency target can be missed with plenty of apparent headroom. The rule that follows is simple: change what the evidence names, and then measure again.

The simplest way to add capacity to the application tier is to run several identical copies behind a load balancer. That works when no copy holds something the others need. The first thing that breaks it is session state. If a user's session lives in the memory of one replica, their next request may land on another replica that has never heard of them. So sessions move to a shared store, or into signed tokens that the client carries with each request. The second thing is less obvious: connection pools. Each replica keeps a pool of connections to the database, say twenty. Three replicas hold sixty connections. If the database allows a hundred, which we assume here, that is fine. But growing to six replicas would want a hundred and twenty connections, and some of them would simply fail. So the pool is a capacity budget that has to be planned across all replicas, not a configuration detail. The general pattern is worth remembering: scaling one tier moves the pressure onto whatever that tier depends on.

A cache stores copies of data closer to where it is needed, and the first decision is where. A browser or edge cache is closest to the user but gives us the least control. An in-process cache is the fastest, but every application replica holds its own copy. A shared cache holds one copy for everyone, at the cost of an extra network hop. The most common read pattern is cache-aside. The application checks the cache first. On a miss, it reads from the database and then fills the cache for next time. Here is the arithmetic, using hypothetical numbers. If one thousand reads per second arrive and eighty percent of them hit the cache, then only two hundred reads per second reach the database. Our own peak of eleven hundred and fifty-seven reads a second would leave about two hundred and thirty-one. Writes need a policy as well. Write-through updates the cache and the database together. Invalidating on write simply deletes the cache key and lets the next read refill it. Write-back is fast, but data acknowledged to the client can be lost if the cache fails before it reaches the database.

Every cache can serve data that is out of date, so the real design question is how out of date is acceptable. Follow the timeline. The cache and the database both hold address A. The owner edits the link, and the database now says address B. Until something changes the cache entry, visitors keep receiving A. There are two controls. Expiry, usually called a time to live, bounds the staleness: if entries live for sixty seconds, which we assume here, no one waits longer than that. Invalidation deletes or updates the key when the data changes, so the next read loads the new value. Each has a trade-off. A short expiry gives fresher data but more misses, which means more load on the database. Invalidation gives fresher data, but the delete itself can fail, or it can race with a concurrent read that is just refilling the cache with the old value. A sensible design uses both: invalidate on write, and keep a time to live as a safety net. And always go back to the requirement. A redirect may tolerate a minute of staleness, but a link removed for abuse may not.

A cache improves the average case, but it brings its own failure modes. The first is the hot key. Popularity is skewed, so in the assumed distribution shown here, the single most visited link draws about twenty-two percent of all requests. If that key lives on one cache node, that node takes a fifth of the traffic by itself. The second is the stampede. When a popular entry expires, many requests miss at the same moment, and all of them go to the database to refill it. The third is the outage. If the cache fails or is restarted empty, every read falls through, and a database sized for two hundred reads a second suddenly faces one thousand. The defences follow from the failures. Replicate hot keys, or keep them in a small local cache. Coalesce concurrent misses, so one request refills the entry while the others wait. Add jitter to expiry times, so entries do not all die together. And when the database is at risk, serve slightly stale data or shed load, rather than letting everything fail.

When the database's read load is the problem, replication is the next tool. Writes go to one primary, and replicas copy its changes and serve reads. Adding replicas adds read capacity, but it does nothing for write capacity, because every write still goes to the primary. The price is lag. With asynchronous replication, a replica trails the primary by some amount, which we assume here is between two tenths of a second and two seconds. That creates a surprising bug: an owner creates a link, the write lands on the primary, and when they immediately follow it, the read goes to a replica that has not yet received the row, so they see a not-found. The fix is to read from the primary just after a write, or to track what the replica has applied before trusting it. Replicas also support failover. If the primary fails, a replica can be promoted. But writes that the primary acknowledged and had not yet copied may be lost, or may conflict later, and in the next chapter we examine exactly what that means.

When one machine can no longer hold the data or take the writes, we partition it across several, which is also called sharding. The most important decision is the shard key. A good key spreads data and load evenly, and it appears in the most frequent queries. For our links the natural choice is the code, because every redirect looks up by code. There are three common schemes. Hashing the key gives an even spread, but you lose efficient range queries. Splitting by ranges of the key allows range queries, but popular ranges become hot. A directory, a lookup table that says where each key lives, is flexible, but it is one more component that must stay available. Now the price. The shard key makes one access pattern cheap and others expensive. Redirects go to exactly one shard. But listing links by owner does not carry the code, so the query must ask every shard and combine the answers. And a transaction that touches two shards is hard to make correct. Choose the key for the access pattern that matters most.

Partitioning raises three practical problems. The first is the hot partition. Spreading keys evenly does not spread load evenly, because one viral link sends all of its traffic to a single shard. The answer is to cache that key, split it across several, or give it dedicated replicas. The second is rebalancing. Suppose we assign each key to a shard by taking its hash modulo the number of shards, and we go from four shards to five. A key stays where it was only if its hash gives the same remainder both ways, which happens for just one key in five. So about eighty percent of all keys must move. That is a very expensive way to add capacity. The better design hashes keys into many small fixed partitions, say sixty-four, and keeps a table mapping partitions to nodes. Adding a node moves only about thirteen of the sixty-four partitions, roughly twenty percent. The third problem is routing. Something, a router or a client library, must map key to partition to node, and that mapping must itself be kept available and consistent.

Let us finish by scaling the system in stages, where each change is justified by evidence. All of the evidence here is supplied for the exercise and is hypothetical. In stage one, the database processor is at eighty-five percent at our peak of eleven hundred and fifty-seven reads a second. The evidence names the database, so we add a cache, and assuming an eighty percent hit rate, database reads fall to about two hundred and thirty-one a second. But the change introduces new failure modes: stale reads, and a cold start when the cache is empty. In stage two, traffic has quadrupled and the application servers are at ninety percent. The evidence names the application tier, so we add replicas, and we must watch the database connection budget. In stage three, click writes reach four thousand a second against a primary that handles about fifteen hundred. Now the evidence does justify partitioning, by code. And again there are new risks, hot shards and queries that cross shards. Notice what we did not do: we did not shard at stage one, because the evidence never asked for it. Next, we ask what correctness guarantees survive all these copies.

On a single machine, a program mostly either works or crashes. A distributed system has a nastier property: parts of it can fail while other parts carry on. Suppose a caller asks node B something and hears nothing back. What does that silence mean? The node may have crashed and will never answer. It may be alive but slow, perhaps overloaded, paused for housekeeping, or swapping memory. Or the node may be perfectly healthy and the network between you and it may be cut. From the caller's side, all three look exactly the same. So a failure detector, usually just a timeout, is only a guess. If the timeout is too short, you declare a live node dead. If it is too long, you take ages to notice a real crash. Neither mistake can be eliminated, only traded off. That has a serious consequence. If a node is wrongly declared dead, and another is promoted to replace it, you can end up with two nodes both acting as the leader. The rest of this chapter is about designing so that such mistakes do not corrupt data.

To say whether a distributed system is correct, we need something more precise than a feeling. A history records what each client did and what it saw, along with when each operation started and ended. Look at this small example, on a single register that starts at zero. Client A starts writing the value one at time one, and its write returns at time three. Client B reads in the middle, while the write is still in progress. Because the operations overlap, B may see zero or one, and both answers are legal. Now client C starts a read at time four, after A's write has completely finished, and gets zero. That is a violation. The rule, called linearizability, says each operation must appear to take effect at a single instant somewhere between its start and its end, so a read that begins after a write has finished must not see an older value. The attraction of histories is that they describe correctness without describing the implementation, and a single bad history is a counterexample that proves a system does not meet the guarantee.

Two kinds of property matter in distributed systems, and it helps to keep them apart. A safety property says that nothing bad ever happens. Two examples are that there are never two leaders in the same term, and that stock never drops below zero. You can point at a safety violation: there is a specific moment where the bad thing happened. A liveness property says that something good eventually happens, such as a leader eventually being elected, or every request eventually being answered. You cannot point at a single moment of violation, because it is only violated by a never-ending absence of progress. The distinction matters most during a partition. A server that cannot reach a majority of its peers can refuse to decide anything. That preserves safety, because no conflicting decisions are made, but it costs liveness, because requests on that side stall until the partition heals. The usual habit is to protect safety first. A system that is briefly stuck can recover, but a system that has made two conflicting decisions may not be able to.

People say consistency to mean at least three different things, and mixing them up causes real design errors. The first is replication consistency. It asks whether the copies of one object agree. At the strong end, linearizable means the object behaves as though there is a single copy. At the weak end, eventual consistency means the copies will agree once writes stop. The second is transaction isolation, which asks whether concurrent transactions interfere with one another. Serializable isolation means the result is as if the transactions ran one after another. Snapshot isolation is weaker and allows an anomaly called write skew. The third is session guarantees, which ask what a single client sees across its own requests. Read your writes means a client sees its own updates. Monotonic reads means it never sees data go backwards in time. The key point is that these are different axes. A serializable database is not necessarily linearizable, and a replica can still be stale even when transactions are isolated. Improving one axis does not improve the others.

CAP is often quoted and often misunderstood, so let us state it carefully. In the model used by Gilbert and Lynch, a service cannot simultaneously guarantee linearizable consistency, availability of every request, and tolerance of network partitions. Since networks do partition, partition tolerance is not really optional, and so the real choice arises only while a partition is happening: refuse or wait to stay consistent, or answer anyway and risk stale or diverging data. Several misconceptions follow from the slogan pick any two of three. It hides that partition tolerance is not a choice. It suggests that CAP describes normal operation, when it says nothing about it. And its terms are narrow, so real systems cannot be sorted neatly into CP or AP. A useful extension is the PACELC framing, associated with Daniel Abadi. It says: if there is a partition, choose between availability and consistency; else, in normal operation, choose between latency and consistency. Treat it as a lens for asking questions about a design, not as a label to stick on products.

A quorum system tries to get consistent reads from a set of unreliable replicas. Suppose there are N replicas. A write is acknowledged only after W of them have stored it, and a read asks R of them. If W plus R is greater than N, then any set of replicas read must share at least one replica with any set that was written, so the read cannot miss the latest acknowledged write entirely. In our example there are three replicas, and both writes and reads use two. Four is greater than three, so any two replicas you read include at least one that has version two. That is a useful property, but it has limits that are easy to forget. Overlap is necessary, not sufficient, for linearizable reads. A write that fails halfway can leave some replicas ahead of others. Sloppy quorums, which accept other nodes when the usual ones are unreachable, weaken the overlap during failures. And two concurrent writes still need an explicit rule for resolving the conflict. So quorums are a building block, not a full answer.

Consensus is the problem of getting a group of servers to agree on a sequence of decisions even though some of them may fail. Raft is one well-known design, and here is a conceptual walkthrough with three servers. This is simplified and is not a specification. In normal operation, the servers first elect a leader. Time is divided into terms, and in term two a candidate wins with votes from two of the three servers, a majority. A client command goes to the leader, which appends it to its log and sends it to the followers. Once the entry is stored on a majority, it is committed and can be applied. Now suppose the leader crashes. The followers hear nothing, and after a timeout one of them starts a new election in term three. It needs votes from a majority, and a server only votes for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, which is what ensures committed entries survive. Entries that never reached a majority may be lost. The cost is that progress needs a majority: with three servers, one failure is tolerated.

Ordering events across machines is harder than it sounds, because every machine has its own clock, and the clocks disagree. Machines drift, and for the sake of the example we assume skew of up to forty milliseconds. That is enough to cause real problems. If a system resolves conflicting writes by keeping whichever has the later timestamp, a write that happened second can carry an earlier timestamp and be silently discarded. Physical clocks remain very useful for logs and for expiry times, but not for deciding which event came first. Logical clocks take a different approach and order events by causality instead. A Lamport clock is just a counter at each process. It increases on every event, travels with every message, and on receipt jumps to the larger of the two values plus one. If event e causes event f, the clock value for e is smaller than for f. The reverse is not true: a smaller value proves nothing. Vector clocks go further and can tell that two events were concurrent. So order by causality whenever correctness depends on order.

Sometimes one operation must change data held by several participants, and either all of them must commit or none. An atomic commit protocol exists for this, and the best known is two-phase commit. In the first phase, a coordinator asks every participant to prepare, and each replies yes or no. A yes vote is a promise: the participant has made its changes durable and can no longer decide on its own. In the second phase, if every vote was yes the coordinator announces commit, and otherwise it announces abort. This gives a clean all-or-nothing outcome when everything works. The weakness is in the gap between the phases. If the coordinator crashes after the votes are in and before the decision is announced, the participants are in doubt. They cannot safely commit, because the decision might have been abort, and they cannot safely abort, because it might have been commit. So they hold their locks and wait for the coordinator to recover, and other requests queue behind them. Two-phase commit buys atomicity at the price of blocking, which is why many designs try to avoid it.

Here is a very common problem. When a business change happens, such as reserving stock, we usually also want to publish an event so other parts of the system can react. But the database and the message broker are two separate systems with no shared transaction. If the service updates the database and then crashes before publishing, the change happened but nobody was told. If it publishes first and then crashes, the event went out for a change that never happened. The transactional outbox solves the dual write by using only one system at first. In a single local database transaction, the service changes the data and also inserts a row into an outbox table describing the event, so both rows commit or neither does. A separate relay process then reads unsent rows, publishes them, and marks them as sent. Be careful about what this does not fix. If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking the row, it will publish that event again. So delivery is at-least-once, and consumers must be able to handle duplicates, which is the subject of the next chapter.

Let us end with three histories of one inventory item, where the rule is that we must never sell more than we have, and stock is one. In the first history, two buyers read a stock of one at the same moment. Each decides to sell, each writes zero, and the item has been sold twice. That is a failure of transaction isolation, and the fix is an atomic conditional update that only decrements when the stock is still above zero, so the database decides which buyer wins. In the second history, the sale has completed on the primary, but the product page reads from a replica that is still behind, so it keeps offering the item. The transactions were fine here. What failed was replication consistency. In the third history, the primary acknowledges a sale and then crashes before copying it to anyone, and a replica that never saw the sale is promoted. An acknowledged write has been lost, which is a failure of durability. The fix is to wait for a quorum before acknowledging. The lesson is to name which axis failed, because the fixes are completely different. Next, we apply these guarantees to asynchronous work.

So far, our redirect service has answered everything synchronously. But some work does not need to happen while the visitor waits, such as counting clicks or sending notifications. For that we move messages between components, and there are three common shapes. A queue gives each message to exactly one consumer and deletes it once it is acknowledged. That suits tasks, like sending an email. Publish and subscribe gives every subscriber its own copy of each message, which suits fan-out: our analytics and our notifications both want to hear about each click. A retained event stream is an append-only log kept for some retention period. Readers track their own position in it, and can go back and replay. Real products blur these lines, so rather than memorising product names, ask the questions. Who should receive each message? What happens to it afterwards? Do we ever need to read it again? If the work is for one worker, use a queue. If many independent readers need it, use publish and subscribe. If you may need to reprocess, keep a stream.

A single log can only be read so fast, so streams are split into partitions. A topic of clicks, for example, might have three partitions, and each partition is an ordered log. When the producer publishes an event, it chooses a key, and here the key is the link code. Messages with the same key always go to the same partition. That is how we keep one link's events in order. A consumer group then reads the topic together. Each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, so adding consumers scales the work, up to the number of partitions. Notice the ordering scope. Order holds within a partition, not across them, so one link's clicks stay in order, but there is no global order across all links. That is usually all we need, but you must decide it deliberately. Finally, retention bounds how far back anyone can replay. We assume seven days. And remember skew from chapter four: one very popular link means one very busy partition, however many partitions we add.

The two shapes record a consumer's progress in different ways, and that difference decides what you can do after something goes wrong. In a queue, the broker tracks each message. It delivers a message, the consumer works on it, and when the consumer sends an acknowledgement the broker deletes it. If the consumer never acknowledges, the broker redelivers it. Once acknowledged, the message is gone, so there is no replay. In a stream, the log is untouched. The consumer reads at an offset, which is simply its position in the log, does its work, and then commits the next offset. Because the log is retained, the consumer can rewind the offset and replay, for example after fixing a bug or to build a new view. Notice one subtle point. The offset must be committed only after the effect has been applied. If we commit first and crash, the effect is lost, because the consumer will resume past it. So progress is a position, owned by the consumer, and the trade-off is simple: a queue forgets what it delivered, while a stream remembers, at the cost of storage.

A delivery guarantee describes what happens when something crashes, and the answer depends on where the acknowledgement sits relative to the work. Look at the consumer. It receives a message, applies the effect, and acknowledges. If it crashes before the effect, nothing happened and redelivery is harmless. If it crashes after the effect but before the acknowledgement, the broker will deliver the message again, and the effect is duplicated. Now compare the three guarantees. At most once acknowledges first, so a crash loses the message. At least once acknowledges last, so a crash repeats it. Exactly once sounds ideal, but treat the phrase with suspicion. It usually means effectively once, and its scope is often limited to work inside one system, such as reading from a log and writing back to the same store. An outside effect, like sending an email or charging a card, is beyond that boundary. So the practical choice is to use at least once delivery, and make the consumer idempotent so that a duplicate does no harm.

If delivery is at least once, then duplicates will happen, and the consumer must make them harmless. The standard technique is a deduplication key. Every event carries a unique identifier. When the consumer processes an event, it records that identifier in a processed table, and it does so in the same transaction as the effect. Then either both happen or neither does. When a duplicate arrives, the insert into the processed table finds the identifier already there, inserts nothing, and the consumer skips the effect and acknowledges. Some operations are naturally idempotent. Setting a status to shipped can safely repeat, but adding one to a counter cannot, unless it is protected by a key. There is a limit you must plan for. The processed table cannot grow forever, so we prune it, and here we assume seven days. A duplicate that arrives after that would be applied again. So the retention period of the identifiers must be longer than the longest possible redelivery delay, and that is a requirement to state and to test.

Not every failure is temporary. Most are, so the first response is to retry with backoff and jitter, as we saw in chapter two, up to a limit, which we assume is five attempts. Usually a retry succeeds. But some messages fail every single time, perhaps because their content is malformed or triggers a bug. These are poison messages. If we retry them forever, they loop endlessly, and in an ordered partition they can block everything behind them. So after the limit, we move the message aside into a dead-letter queue. It is parked, not lost. Then the recovery is a human process. An alert fires when the dead-letter queue has messages in it. Someone inspects them, fixes the code or the data, and then redrives the messages back into the main flow. That redrive is only safe because our consumers are idempotent, so reprocessing a message that was partly handled does no harm. One more consequence: moving a message aside breaks strict ordering for that key, so you need to decide whether that is acceptable for your data.

Asynchronous systems have a new failure mode: the work arrives faster than it is done. Here is the arithmetic, using assumed rates. At our peak, one thousand one hundred and fifty-seven messages a second arrive, but the consumers can only handle one thousand. The backlog therefore grows by one hundred and fifty-seven a second, and after a ten-minute burst, ninety-four thousand two hundred messages are waiting. That is not a disaster by itself. When the burst ends and arrival falls back to two hundred and thirty-one a second, the consumers have spare capacity of seven hundred and sixty-nine a second, and the backlog drains in about a hundred and twenty-two seconds. But you must watch how old the oldest message is, because that is the delay users feel. There are three standard responses. Backpressure slows or rejects producers when queues grow long. Batching processes many messages per call, which raises throughput at the cost of latency. And materialised views precompute what readers need, so reads do not wait on the backlog. Watch queue depth and the age of the oldest message.

When a business process spans several services, such as an order that must reserve stock, take payment, and ship, we cannot wrap it all in one transaction. Instead, we model it as a state machine. An order is in exactly one state at a time: created, paid, shipped, or failed, and only the listed transitions are allowed. Then we choose how the steps are coordinated. With orchestration, a single coordinator tells each service what to do next. The whole flow is in one place, so it is easy to follow, but the coordinator becomes a central dependency that must stay available. With choreography, there is no coordinator. Each service reacts to the events of the others. That is loosely coupled, but the overall flow is implicit and harder to see and debug. Failures need a plan too. If shipping fails after payment succeeded, we run compensating actions, refunding the card and releasing the stock. But understand what that is. Compensation is a new action going forward, not an atomic rollback. The charge really happened, and the customer may have seen it.

Let us finish by assembling the pieces for click analytics and notifications. When a visitor follows a link, the redirect service records a click event, and it writes that event using the transactional outbox from chapter five, so the event cannot be lost between the database and the broker. The event carries a unique identifier. A relay publishes it to a topic called clicks, which has three partitions keyed by link code, so each link's clicks stay in order. Two consumer groups each receive a copy. One builds daily counts per link, and the other sends milestone notifications. Now trace the failures. If a consumer crashes, it resumes from its committed offset, and any duplicate is skipped using the event identifier. If an event is poison, it is retried five times and then dead-lettered, and an alert fires. If the rollup falls behind, dashboards show stale numbers for a few minutes, which we have decided is acceptable. Most importantly, the redirect never waits for analytics, so a slow consumer cannot slow down a visitor. Next, we decide which responsibilities should live together and which should be separate services.

Before deciding how to deploy anything, we have to decide where one responsibility ends and another begins. In our system there are at least three: creating and resolving links, counting clicks, and managing owners with their keys and quotas. Each is a bounded context, a part of the system within which terms have one meaning. The word link, for example, means a short code that redirects in the links context, but in analytics it is just a label to count against. Two ideas help us judge a boundary. Cohesion is how strongly the things inside belong together, meaning they change together. Coupling is how much one part has to know about another. We want high cohesion inside a boundary and low coupling across it. There are three practical tests. Do these things change together? Does a single team own them? And can one fail without taking the others down? A warning to finish: boundaries drawn by technology layer, like putting all the databases in one place, cut straight through responsibilities and make every change touch everything.

Once we know the responsibilities, we can choose how to package them. Here is the same subsystem drawn two ways. In a modular monolith, the links and analytics modules live in a single deployable. Each module exposes only a public interface and keeps its internals private, so a call between them is just a function call. There is one database, but each module owns its own schema. As independent services, the same two parts are released and scaled separately, and they fail separately. A call between them now crosses a network, which means it can be slow, can be lost, and can meet a version of the other side it does not expect. And each service must own its own data, so there are no shared tables. This is the trade-off. Services buy independent change and independent scaling, but they cost network failure modes, versioned contracts, and a great deal more operational work. A monolith is not a failure to modernise. For our case, one team and a modest load, a modular monolith fits well, and we should split only for a real need, not for fashion.

When parts of a system talk to each other, the agreement between them is a contract, and contracts need owners. The owner of a service publishes the contract and versions it, and consumers depend on the contract, never on the service's internal tables. Within a version, changes are additive only: new optional fields are fine, and a breaking change ships as a new version running alongside the old. Each service, and its data, should have one team that owns it. Shared ownership usually means nobody's. Now look at what happens when services call each other in a chain. Suppose a single redirect depends synchronously on four services, and each is ninety-nine point nine percent available, which is an assumption for this example. The chance that all four answer is point nine nine nine to the fourth power, about ninety-nine point six percent. That is already below the ninety-nine point nine percent target we set in chapter one, and we have not added a single bug. Latency adds up along the chain and failures multiply. The remedies are to shorten the chain: cache an answer, make a call asynchronous, or remove a hop.

Two patterns are frequently mentioned together and frequently confused. CQRS, command query responsibility segregation, means separating the model you write to from the model you read from. In our system, the links table could be the write model, and a statistics view built from it could be a read model shaped for the screens that need it. Event sourcing is a different idea. Instead of storing the current state, you store the changes as an append-only log of events, and you derive the current state by replaying them. These are independent. You can have CQRS with ordinary tables, and a plain table plus a read view is already CQRS. Event sourcing does not require separate read models, although it often uses them. Do they earn their place? They do when the read and write shapes really differ, or when history is itself a requirement, such as an audit trail or views you must be able to rebuild. They do not when the need is plain create and read, where one table suffices. And remember that an event log keeps old event shapes forever, so you must always be able to read them.

A live system cannot be paused while we change it, so every change has to be made in steps that are compatible with what is already running. The standard approach for a schema is called expand and contract. First, expand: add the new column or field, optional and unused, so old code keeps working because it ignores it. Second, dual write: have the new code write both the old and the new, and backfill old rows in small batches. Third, switch reads: move readers to the new field, and verify that it matches the old. Fourth, contract: stop writing the old field and, only after a quiet period, drop it. Why so many steps? Because deploys are not instant. For a while, old and new versions of the code run side by side, and each must work against the same data. It also means every step can be rolled back until the final contract step. The same shape appears elsewhere. For an API, add a new version, run both, and retire the old. For a boundary, route a small slice of calls to the new service first, and grow it as confidence builds.

Let us end with a worked decision, and the right answer here is to keep things as they are. The question is whether analytics should become its own service. The evidence we have, all assumed, is that one team owns the system, the load is two hundred and thirty-one requests a second on average and eleven hundred and fifty-seven at peak, and click processing is already asynchronous, as we designed in chapter six. Option A is to extract an analytics service. That would gain independent scaling and independent releases, but it would cost network failures, contract versions to maintain, on-call load, and data split across two stores with no shared transaction. Option B is to stay inside the modular monolith and enforce the module boundary, which is cheap and keeps transactions local. Nothing in the evidence shows a benefit from extraction, so we choose B, and we write that down in a decision record. The record also says when to revisit: if analytics needs its own scale, its own owner, or its own release cadence. Next, we make the whole system observable, secure, and recoverable.

Reliability is only useful once it is a number that someone can check. A service level indicator, or SLI, is a measured ratio: good events divided by valid events, over a stated window. The definition must say exactly what counts, and our assumed one counts redirect requests at the load balancer, with server errors as the failures. A service level objective, or SLO, is the target for that ratio. A service level agreement, or SLA, is a contract with consequences, and it is usually looser than the internal objective so that you have room before you owe anyone anything. Here is a worked example with assumed numbers. Six hundred million redirects in thirty days, and an objective of ninety-nine point nine percent. The error budget is the point one percent that is left, which is six hundred thousand failed requests. If one hundred and fifty thousand have failed this month, the indicator is ninety-nine point nine seven five percent and a quarter of the budget is spent. The budget guides decisions: while some remains, ship changes; when it is gone, slow down and fix reliability. Finally, keep a capacity margin. Using the queueing intuition from chapter four, we plan to stay under about seventy percent utilisation at peak.

When something goes wrong, you can only fix what you can see, and there are three kinds of signal. Metrics are numbers over time, which makes them cheap and ideal for alerting. Logs are discrete events with detail, such as a particular failure and its error message. Traces follow one request through the whole system, showing where its time went. They are most useful when they are joined together. Look at the example. An alert rule watches the error ratio and pages when it stays above two percent for three minutes. That tells us something is wrong. The log lines show database timeouts and carry a trace identifier. And the trace for that identifier shows that almost all of a twelve-hundred-millisecond request was spent in one database query. Following the identifier took us from symptom to cause. A word about alerts. A good alert is actionable: it describes something users feel, it has an owner, it links a runbook, and it asks someone to do something now. Causes like high processor use belong on dashboards or in tickets, because paging people for things that need no action teaches them to ignore pages.

A failing dependency is dangerous mainly because of what it does to everything that calls it. Callers wait, threads pile up, and soon the healthy parts are stuck too. Four patterns contain the damage. A circuit breaker watches calls to a dependency. While things work, it is closed and calls flow. After repeated failures it opens, and calls fail immediately instead of waiting, giving the dependency room to recover. After a pause, which we assume is thirty seconds, it goes half-open and lets one trial call through. If that succeeds, it closes again. Bulkheads give each dependency its own pool of threads or connections, so a slow dependency can exhaust only its own pool, not everyone's. Load shedding rejects low-priority work early, when the system is overloaded, so the important work still completes. And graceful degradation means deciding in advance what is optional. Our redirect must keep working even if analytics is down, and a stale cached redirect is better than none. The key is deciding which functions are essential before the failure arrives.

Security starts with a habit of asking questions, and a common framing uses four. What are we building? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? And did we do a good enough job? To answer them, draw the system and mark the trust boundaries, which are the places where data crosses from something we do not control into something we do. For us, everything arriving from the internet is untrusted input. Now ask what can go wrong for a link service in particular. People can abuse it to create spam and phishing links in bulk. They can enumerate it, guessing codes to discover destinations that were meant to be quiet. And they can create links whose targets lead to malware, using our domain's good name. Each threat gets a response. Rate limits slow bulk creation. Validation and blocklists reject dangerous targets. And codes that are hard to guess make enumeration expensive, though remember from chapter three that an unguessable code is not a secret, so it must never be the only thing protecting something private.

Four controls are often blurred together, so let us separate them by the question each answers. Authentication asks who is calling. We verify an API key or token on every request, and we never trust a claim a client makes about itself. Authorisation asks what that caller may do, once we know who they are. For example, an owner may change only their own links, so the server must check the owner identifier on every edit, and it must not rely on the client to send the right one. Grant each caller the least privilege that lets it do its job. Secrets, such as database passwords and signing keys, must not live in source code. Inject them at runtime, rotate them, limit who can read them, and never write them to logs, because logs travel widely. Finally, encryption. In transit, we use TLS on every hop, and at rest we encrypt storage and backups. But encryption is not access control: if a service holds the key, then whoever controls that service can read the data. Each control answers its own question, and none of them substitutes for another.

Limits protect the system from overload and from abuse, and a token bucket is a simple, widely used way to enforce them. Here is our assumed rule: no more than one hundred link creations per owner per hour, with bursts allowed. The bucket holds ten tokens, and every create spends one. Tokens refill at one hundred an hour, which works out to one token every thirty-six seconds. Suppose an owner makes ten creates at once. All ten succeed and the bucket is empty. The eleventh is rejected with a too-many-requests response, and a retry-after header says to wait thirty-six seconds. The plot shows the bucket refilling steadily, and it is full again after three hundred and sixty seconds. That means the long-run rate can never exceed the refill rate, while short bursts are still allowed, which is friendlier to legitimate users. A quota is a separate idea: a cap over a longer period, such as a day. And abuse controls look for patterns, like thousands of near-identical links, not just counts. Apply limits per key, at the edge, before expensive work is done.

Most outages follow a change, so how we ship changes matters as much as the code. The safest approach is a canary release. We deploy the new version to a small slice of traffic, say one percent, and watch it for a fixed time, assumed here to be ten minutes. We compare its error ratio and latency against the baseline running the old version. If it looks healthy, we promote it gradually: ten percent, then fifty, then everything, watching at each step. If it looks worse, we roll back automatically to the previous version, and only a small number of users ever saw the problem. Two things make this work. First, configuration changes are code. A configuration value can break a system as surely as a bug can, so it deserves the same review, validation, staging, and gradual rollout. Second, rollback must be boring. That means the previous version is still deployable, and schema changes were made in the compatible steps we saw in chapter seven, so the old code can still run against the new data.

A backup is only useful if you can restore from it fast enough, and without losing too much. Two numbers capture the requirement. The recovery time objective, or RTO, is how long recovery may take. The recovery point objective, or RPO, is how much recent data we may lose. Suppose our assumed requirement is an RTO of one hour and an RPO of five minutes. Now compare three options, using figures we also assume, which in real life would come from restore drills. A nightly backup might take four hours to restore and lose up to twenty-four hours of data, so it misses both. Promoting a replica takes about fifteen minutes and loses only a few seconds, so it meets both, but it copies a bad delete as faithfully as any other change. Point-in-time recovery, which replays archived logs, loses at most five minutes but might take two hours, so it meets the data target and misses the time target. No single option covers everything. A replica handles machine loss, and point-in-time recovery handles mistakes. And whichever you choose, rehearse the restore, because an untested restore is a hope, not a plan.

Redundancy only helps if the copies do not fail together, so we reason about failure domains: the sets of things that fail at the same time. From small to large, a process can crash, a machine or rack can fail, a whole zone, which is roughly a data-centre building, can lose power or networking, and a whole region can be unavailable. Each recovery choice survives up to a certain size of domain. Running across multiple zones in one region survives the loss of a zone, with recovery in minutes. A warm standby in another region survives losing a whole region, but recovery takes longer, here assumed to be about an hour, because data must be current and traffic must be redirected. An active-active design, serving from several regions at once, gives near-zero recovery but is the hardest to keep consistent, as we saw in chapter five. Each step up costs more money and more complexity. So match the choice to the recovery time and recovery point you actually need, not to ambition.

Let us read an outage timeline, using assumed times. At nine o'clock a configuration change ships to every server at once. At four minutes past, redirects begin to fail. The alert fires at seven minutes past, because the rule needed three minutes above two percent. The on-call engineer finds the cause, a bad connection limit in the configuration, at twenty past. Rollback begins at twenty-five past, and service is restored at thirty-one minutes past. So the impact lasted twenty-seven minutes. At our average rate of two hundred and thirty-one requests a second, that is about three hundred and seventy-five thousand failed requests, which uses sixty-two and a half percent of the monthly error budget in a single morning. Now compare the recovery alternatives. Rolling back returns us to a known good state and is the fastest, so it was chosen. Fixing forward means writing and testing a new change under pressure, with unknown time and new risk. And failing over to a second region would not help at all, because the same bad configuration is deployed there too. Failover protects against failed infrastructure, not against a faulty change.

After the incident is over, the most valuable work begins: understanding why it happened, so the next one is less likely or less damaging. A good review looks for contributing causes, plural, rather than a single root cause or a single person to blame. In our example, several things combined. The configuration value was not validated, so a bad one was accepted. The change shipped to every server at once, with no canary to catch it on a small slice. And the alert needed three minutes to fire, with no runbook for that symptom, which cost more time. Each cause suggests a preventive action. Validate configuration, roll it out gradually, tighten the alert window, and write the runbook. Then be honest about residual risk. Some bad changes will still pass every test, so we accept that risk, keep watching for it, and say so explicitly. Finally, how to write it up: a timeline, the impact, the causes, and actions with owners and dates, all written about the system and not about people. This course has described operational reasoning only. It is not an assessment of anyone's performance.

Over eight chapters we have built up a set of ideas. Now we put them into a single repeatable method with four stages. First, understand the problem: write down the requirements, functional and quality, and then estimate traffic, data, and peak demand. Second, shape the solution: define the operations and the data, and choose the simplest architecture that fits. Third, stress it: find the dominant bottleneck, the thing that saturates first, and trace what happens when each part fails. Fourth, decide: compare the alternatives, including their cost, and record the decision. A decision record is short. It states the question and the context along with the assumptions, the options that were considered, the choice, why it was chosen in terms of requirements and evidence, and when to revisit it. That last part matters, because the right answer today may not be the right answer when the workload or the requirements change. A few habits carry through every stage. State your assumptions and label your estimates. Start simple, and add a mechanism only for a named requirement. And always say what the design does when each part fails.

A design is never finished, because the requirements change. Let us revisit the URL shortener under two assumed changes. First, traffic grows tenfold, to two hundred million redirects a day. That is about two thousand three hundred and fifteen requests a second on average, and eleven thousand five hundred and seventy-four at a five times peak. Second, there is a new correctness requirement: abusive links must stop redirecting within five seconds. Look at what breaks. Our cache has a sixty-second time to live, so a link taken down for abuse could keep redirecting visitors for up to a minute. That violates the new requirement. And the load has changed too. At an eighty percent hit rate, the database now sees about two thousand three hundred reads a second, ten times what it did in chapter four. The revision keeps the cache but changes how it is kept correct. On takedown, an event purges the caches, and we keep the sixty-second expiry only as a safety net. We add read replicas for the extra load, and we still do not shard, because nothing yet requires it. And we state what is unresolved: a purge can fail, and the expiry limits how long the damage lasts.

The URL shortener has been our running example, but it is not a template. Different systems are dominated by different concerns, and a good designer changes the answer to match. Take chat. Suppose ten million daily users send forty messages each. That is four hundred million messages a day, about four thousand six hundred and thirty a second on average. The challenge is delivering quickly with order preserved within a conversation, so we use persistent connections and key messages by conversation. A news feed is read-heavy: two hundred million feed loads a day. The bottleneck is fan-out, so a hybrid approach writes into followers' feeds for most accounts, and reads on demand for very popular ones. File storage is about volume. One million uploads of five megabytes is five terabytes a day. Bandwidth and cost dominate, so bytes go to an object store and only metadata goes in a database. And payments are the surprise: only about one a second, yet the hardest, because correctness is everything. They need idempotency keys, a ledger, reconciliation, and a policy of failing closed. Same method, four very different architectures.

Now let us work one design through the whole method, using file storage, with every number assumed. The flow is this. When a client wants to upload, the API does not take the bytes. It returns signed addresses, and the client sends the file in chunks directly to the object store. When all the parts are in, a commit step verifies them and only then writes a metadata row to the database. Downloads are served through a content delivery network, close to the users. Now the estimates. One million uploads of five megabytes each is five terabytes a day, about fifty-eight megabytes a second on average, and about one point eight petabytes a year. At an assumed price of two cents per gigabyte per month, a year of accumulated data costs roughly thirty-six thousand five hundred dollars a month, so cost is a first-class concern. Failure behaviour is explicit. An interrupted upload resumes from the last part. We always write the blob first and the row second, so there is never a row without a file, and a sweeper deletes orphaned blobs. And we rejected three alternatives: storing files in the database, which bloats it, routing bytes through the API, which turns it into a bandwidth bottleneck, and managing our own disks, which makes durability our job.

The last skill is critique: looking at a design, including your own, and saying honestly what is wrong with it. A useful method checks the design against the requirements, then its assumptions, its failure modes, its cost, and its simplicity. For each finding, you state the revision, and, importantly, what the revision still leaves open. Apply that to the file storage design. First, files are stored without any malware scanning. The revision is to scan after upload and before sharing, but that delays sharing. Second, there is no way to delete a file everywhere. The revision removes the row, the blob, and the cached copy, but backups still hold the data for an assumed thirty-five days, which must be disclosed. Third, there is only one region. We can replicate blobs to a second one, but the metadata failover is still manual. Fourth, the cost of downloads is unbounded, so a viral file could be very expensive. Caching and per-file limits help, though limits can annoy legitimate users. Notice that unresolved trade-offs are part of the design, so write them down. To go further, work through unfamiliar designs, read original sources, and study real incident analyses, and remember that practical competence also requires hands-on implementation experience.
